voice_event.speaker: gallic
voice_event.text:
Jesus is our Lord, the crucified one who calls us to himself while we are still ignorant and unwilling, and draws us toward salvation. At Tours this comes to us as a story. The devil came to Martin in his cell dressed in purple, with a crown of gold and jewels, and said, I am Christ. Martin kept silence a long time. Then he said he would not believe that Christ had come unless he came in the form in which he suffered, showing the marks of his wounds. We also met him in the poor. Tours remembered a beggar at a city gate whom everyone passed, and a soldier who cut his one cloak in half for him; that night the soldier saw Christ wearing the half he had given away. Among the brethren at Marseilles the same thing was taught in the fathers' words, from Egypt: an elder broke his fast for two strangers at his door, because receiving Christ in them he ought to refresh him. What he taught that mattered most among us was that without him we can do nothing - the sentence Cassian sets under every virtue a monk feels he has gained, beside the Apostle's not I, but the grace of God with me. And at the sixth hour the spotless Sacrifice, our Lord and Saviour, was offered up to the Father and went up on the cross for the salvation of the whole world, taking away the debt that could not be paid.

**Cassian, Institutes V.26**: I can fast any day. But I am about to walk you on your way, and so I cannot keep you with me for long. When you have gone, I will be able to make up for this food I have taken by a stricter fast. But I cannot always have you with me. And fasting is indeed always in my power. But receiving Christ in you, I ought to refresh Him. When I have sent you on your way, I will be able to maintain a stricter rule in the matter of food. For the sons of the bridegroom cannot fast while the bridegroom is with them. But when the bridegroom shall be taken from them, then they will rightly fast.

glosses.plain_meaning: A real, present, and at times visible adversary. Martin saw him in many shapes and spoke to him. Our elders detect him in a thought we are ashamed to disclose.
glosses.quick_meaning: A real and present enemy, sometimes visible. Martin knew him in any shape and spoke to him. Our elders find him in the thought we are ashamed to tell. Never a figure of speech.
glosses.translational_sense: A modern hearer wants to read our devil as psychology - inner conflict, a shadow, a primitive name for illness. That is the one reading we cannot allow. Ours is a named, embodied, sometimes visible adversary who takes the shapes of the old gods, who can be spoken to and even offered mercy, and who quotes Scripture in church.
false_friend: a metaphor for psychological conflict, "the shadow," or social evil
demons as a primitive explanation for illness
Martin's conversations with the devil as legend

glosses.plain_meaning: The monk's own dwelling, and the place where everything happens to him. There Martin prays, receives saints, and is tempted by a purple-robed devil behind a closed door. There Cassian's junior may not go out without leave, stays all day at his work, and is assailed at noon by the disease that makes him hate the cell itself.
glosses.quick_meaning: The monk's own hut or cave, rarely left except for prayer - where saints and the devil come, and where the wandering heart is held still.
glosses.translational_sense: 'A cell - like a prison, or a private room?' - neither: it is the one place a monk is, a wooden hut or a hollow in the rock he rarely leaves except for prayer, where saints and the devil appear, and in the south a harbour whose barriers hold the wandering heart still by labour and rule - with its own named affliction at noon.
false_friend: a prison cell
a bare private bedroom, with solitude as privacy
a hermitage as retreat from stress

glosses.plain_meaning: A monk, for us, is a man who has cut himself off from marriage, kin, property and the life of the world for a stricter life in Christ's service. The cut shows in his body and his dwelling. But at Tours a soldier still in the ranks could be "regarded as a monk," and so could a bishop in his see.
glosses.quick_meaning: A man cut off from marriage, kin, property and the life of the world for a stricter service of Christ. At Tours even a soldier and a bishop wore the name.
glosses.translational_sense: 'Wasn't a monk by definition cloistered and withdrawn - the opposite of a soldier or a bishop?' - not for us: Martin was called a monk while still under arms and stayed one as bishop of Tours, because the word names a severance from kin, marriage and property kept strictly, not an enclosure, and no written Rule of our own defined him.
false_friend: a cloistered professional religious under a written Rule and an abbot
someone who by definition is not a soldier, not a bishop, and not to be found in a city
medieval monasticism in dress and discipline

glosses.plain_meaning: In Cassian's Marseilles, the help of God without which no effort reaches its goal. Grace "always co-operates with our will"; it goes before the will and follows it; it inspires the first desire and crowns the last perseverance. We hold it together, on purpose, with a will that stays free - in a relation "that cannot be fully grasped by the mind and reason of man."
glosses.quick_meaning: God's help, without which no effort reaches its goal - going before the will, working with it, and requiring it. Held on both sides at once, by design.
glosses.translational_sense: 'So were you on the side of grace or of works - were you semi-Pelagians?' - the label is a sixteenth-century coinage that appears in our own texts only in the editors' notes; what we held was help that co-operates, precedes and requires labour, on both sides at once, declared beyond reason's grasp - and a Representative who resolves it either way has left us.
false_friend: a binary of grace alone versus works, Augustine versus Pelagius, on one side of which we must be placed
semi-Pelagian as a settled verdict
grace as a feeling or a favour
abstract theology unrelated to how anyone lived

figures_used.bridge_line: The soldier who halved his cloak, told Caesar he was now the soldier of Christ, was seized for a see by a crowd and a trick, kept a monk's habits inside the bishop's office, yielded once at Treves and never sat with bishops again, and died on sackcloth and ashes so as not to leave a different example.

dates.display: d. 397, on a peacemaking journey to Condate; a soldier under 'Julian Caesar' in his youth, discharged at a donative; monk 'not far from the town' where Hilary was bishop, then bishop of Tours from an undated election (the monastery across the river founded 'after 371' only on the editorial introduction's word); 'lived sixteen years' after the Treves affair by Gallus's own reckoning

names.name: Cassian, the founder of the houses at Marseilles

figures_used.bridge_line: The man who lived among the fathers of Egypt and brought their words home to Gaul in a book - who told no tales of his own houses and no miracles, but wrote down how a question about grace troubled him and his friend at morning service.

dates.display: travelled in Egypt with Germanus in his youth (the interval to his writing not stated in this world's own documents); founded the twin houses at Marseilles c. 415; wrote the Institutes for Castor before 426 and the Conferences in three parts, Part II (to Honoratus and Eucherius) not later than 426; d. c. 435

confidence.divergence_note: Genuinely shared - all three founding voices, both nodes: Martin sees him, Cassian's elders discern him, Vincent hears him quote Scripture. The visibility of the enemy is Sulpitius's emphasis, and the historicity of the northern appearances is not assessed here (carried by virtus / power's Reported-Experience Status). No Latin lemma sought - common vocabulary; daemonio meridiano is Gibson's editorial Latin at Inst. X.1.

Documented as to existence, office, and reputation: Sulpitius's Life, Letters, Dialogues, and Sacred History within or just after Martin's own lifetime, corroborated independently by Gennadius ch. XIX (ancient text: "monk and bishop," "a man famous for signs and wonders and virtues"). Everything narrated of him rests on one author, so every story is Widely Accepted, never Documented, at the narrative level (Doc_01 §2.2's rule that one ancient witness is not multiple independent sources); the two stories whose narrative claim is the wonder itself are Tier 3. The year of his birth, of the cloak, of the discharge, and of the election are not given in the text (the emperor is "Julian Caesar," the monastery's founding "after 371" only in the editorial introduction). His death in 397 is the horizon's own fixed point. Whether Sulpitius's virtus-organized Life is modelled on the Vita Antonii (Stancliffe, row 18, unread) is open and bears on how much of G6 is the north's own literary form, not on any fact about Martin.

Two voices, both nodes. The rule of the cell (not leaving it, alone or with one other) is Cassian's Egyptian prescription, and whether any Gallic house kept it is not documented. The Latin cella / cellulis reaches us only through the editor's Introduction, in a sentence that is Cardinal Noris's (general reference only), not our own Latin as read.

Contested for the formation portrait (the charitable soldier "regarded not so much as being a soldier as a monk") - the whole tradition's claim about Martin's youth, corroborated by no independent witness inside our own Native corpus; Inferential-Thin for the specific event and for the dream-vision that follows it. Sulpitius did not witness any of this: he met Martin decades later and says he had his information "partly from himself ... and partly from those who had lived with him" (Vita ch. XXV). "The city of Amiens" is Roberts's own main text, naming Sulpitius's "Ambianensium civitas" directly rather than leaving it untranslated - quoted here as part of that main text, not from the endnote (which separately notes the identification as traditional). Roberts's Matt. xxv. 40 cross-reference is editorial apparatus (Registry row 17), not Sulpitius's text. Every quoted phrase was read at its own locus (npnf211 div ii.ii.iii-iv) at Doc_09 construction.

confidence.divergence_note: Documented as an author, a corpus, and a founder: the Institutes (for Castor, before the Conferences), the Conferences in three parts to named Gallic dedicatees (Part II not later than 426 on the vendored edition's own reasoning from Honoratus's title), and Gennadius ch. LXII (ancient text) on the two houses at Marseilles, "one for men and one for women, which are still standing." Contested [CT] is what his Thirteenth Conference meant in relation to Augustine and whether "semi-Pelagian" is fair (Chadwick vs. Casiday, Doc_01 §7) - carried at gallic.term.grace and gallic.term.free-will, not resolved here. The interval between his Egyptian journey and his writing in Gaul is not stated in this world's own documents and is not computed. Three of his texts are absent from the vendored English edition by the translator's own excision (Conf. XII, XXII; Inst. VI - row 11). He never mentions Martin, and no Native voice narrates his reaction to Prosper or Augustine - the controversy he is famous for has no narrative form in any Native voice (Doc_09 §8 item 5). Every locus below read directly at Doc_09.

The best-attested cross-node term in the lexicon: Sulpitius (Tours) and Cassian (Marseilles) use it independently, and Gennadius and Salvian corroborate. Vincent of Lerins never uses it of himself in what was read; that absence is stated, not filled. The three-kinds taxonomy (coenobite, anchorite, Sarabaite) is Cassian's alone and is framed by him as Egypt's own account, not Gaul's.

Contested-Tradition term, two contest types. Meaning: whether Cassian's "co-operates," "precedes" and "inspires us with a good will to begin with" amount to Augustine's prevenient grace or to the position Prosper's Contra Collatorem attacked - the Chadwick (redating Honoratus so that Conf. XIII answers Augustine) versus Casiday (rejecting the redating; little direct polemic) contest, bound to the contested chronology; Cassian's own text says the beginning comes from God in some places and can arise "from our own efforts" in others (XIII.8, XIII.12). Application: whether "semi-Pelagian," a sixteenth-century coinage present in our files only in the editors' apparatus, fairly describes the Massilian position, and whether Vincent and Lerins held it at all (Heurtley's editorial claim, contested). Cross-voice: our own voice (Cassian), the provoking outsider reporting us (Augustine), and a later insider (Faustus, via Gennadius) do not speak in unison. Tours is silent because its corpus closed before the question was posed - an absence, not a disagreement. Faustus's own De gratia is unread beyond a bounded grep, so the in-window Lerins side cannot be stated in its own words.

confidence.divergence_note: Contested for the formation portrait (the charitable soldier "regarded not so much as being a soldier as a monk") - the whole tradition's claim about Martin's youth, corroborated by no independent witness inside our own Native corpus; Inferential-Thin for the specific event and for the dream-vision that follows it. Sulpitius did not witness any of this: he met Martin decades later and says he had his information "partly from himself ... and partly from those who had lived with him" (Vita ch. XXV). "The city of Amiens" is Roberts's own main text, naming Sulpitius's "Ambianensium civitas" directly rather than leaving it untranslated - quoted here as part of that main text, not from the endnote (which separately notes the identification as traditional). Roberts's Matt. xxv. 40 cross-reference is editorial apparatus (Registry row 17), not Sulpitius's text. Every quoted phrase was read at its own locus (npnf211 div ii.ii.iii-iv) at Doc_09 construction.

voice_event.speaker: gallic
voice_event.text:
At the sixth hour he went up on the cross for the salvation of the whole world, made atonement for the sins of mankind, and set free all of us who were bound by a debt that could not be paid, taking it out of the way and nailing it to his cross. At the ninth hour he went down into hell and brought out the captive saints. Dead in the flesh, he was not dead in the spirit; his soul was not left in hell; no one took his life from him, he laid it down himself and took it again. That is what we kept at the hours of prayer. The difference it made is the one our whole life stands on. A man who leaves Caesar's service for Christ's fights the devil in his own heart, where a kingdom is being made ready for the devil or for Christ. The power that raised a dead catechumen at the saint's prayer was Christ's, not the saint's. He calls us to himself while we are still ignorant and unwilling, and draws us toward salvation; and those who perish, perish against his will.

**Cassian, Institutes III.3**: For at the third hour, the Holy Spirit came down upon the apostles. At the sixth hour, Peter went up to the higher parts of the house to pray - that was when he saw the vessel, like a great sheet, let down from heaven by its four corners, and he heard the voice saying to him, Rise, Peter, kill and eat. At that same hour, too, our Lord and Saviour, going up on the cross for the salvation of the whole world, made atonement for the sins of mankind. At the ninth hour, he gave up his spirit and went down to the lower regions of the underworld, to bring back from there the souls of the saints and lead them to paradise.

glosses.translational_sense: Not a short waiting period before a near-default infant baptism: at Tours the state could last years into adult soldiering, and it is where our literature locates the first breaking-through of Martin's power.
false_friend: a brief administrative waiting period before an expected infant baptism

results.message: What does purity of heart mean?

voice_event.speaker: gallic
voice_event.text:
Purity of heart meant the monk's immediate goal, short of the kingdom itself: a heart cleared to charity. It came to us from the fathers of Egypt, through Cassian. He set it down as the thing every fast, vigil, reading and renunciation is aimed at, "as if on a definite mark," like an archer's target. By that mark all of these are ranked as aids to perfection and never as perfection itself. It is the nearer thing - the goal - with the kingdom of heaven as the end beyond it. The whole southern formation program served it. Discretion, the virtue the Egyptians put above all others, is its regulator. The eight faults fought in order are its combats. Labour in the cell, the psalms at the hours, the thought laid bare to the senior - all of it exists to clear the heart to charity. At Tours the words were not used, but the thing was there: the saint kept his mind on prayer even at other work, the way a smith beats his anvil between strokes. The measure of whether a practice helps is whether it clears the heart. The mark stays fixed; the practices are judged by it.

**Cassian, Conferences I.7**: So our profession has, as I have said, its own immediate aim or goal. It moves toward that mark with all care and effort. And if a man does not reach it, his whole effort will have been without fruit and slack. Every art and discipline has some goal or mark - and an end or aim - of its own. Whoever loves that thing with all his heart puts up with every danger, every labor, every cost without trouble. A farmer, through sun and frost, never stops breaking the hard earth with his plough. He has in view the mark and aim of his art - the land cleared of all thorns, soft and without weeds, so that it may return to him more abundant harvests and enrich him with the greatest profit.

glosses.plain_meaning: In Cassian's Marseilles, the immediate goal of the whole monastic life, as distinct from its end, the kingdom of heaven. It is the "definite mark" at which every fast, vigil, reading and renunciation is aimed, "which is charity." By it all of these are ranked as aids to perfection and never as perfection itself.
glosses.quick_meaning: The monk's immediate goal, short of the kingdom itself: a heart cleared to charity. Every fast and vigil is ranked by it as an aid, and never as the point.
glosses.translational_sense: 'Purity of heart - do you mean chastity, or just being sincere?' - neither: we mean the target itself, a state of undistracted charity and "tranquillity of mind" from which the kingdom is reached and by which every fast and vigil is measured and ranked; chastity is one element within it, and our own conference on chastity is missing from our English text.
false_friend: sexual purity or moral spotlessness
a pure heart as sincerity or good intentions
perfection as flawlessness or perfectionism

glosses.plain_meaning: The act that makes a monk: "nothing but the evidence of the cross and of mortification," by which, as Pinufius says, the monk is dead to the world "and its deeds and desires." In the south's received teaching it has three stages. Giving up one's goods, "of what is not our own," is only the first, and "is not enough of itself to confer perfection on the renunciant."
glosses.quick_meaning: The act that makes a monk - a death to the world of which giving up goods is only the first and easiest stage. And the Church still fetches renunciants for its sees.
glosses.translational_sense: 'So renunciation means giving everything up - poverty, celibacy, leaving society for good?' - that is only the first and easiest of three stages for us, "of what is not our own"; the real renunciation is of what belongs to us, our affections and our will, a death "to this world" that extends what every baptized Christian renounced at the font - and after which the Church still comes to fetch the renunciant to be its bishop.
false_friend: giving things up - poverty, celibacy, "detachment" - as the whole of the monastic act
a heroic once-for-all rejection of society
self-denial for its own sake

glosses.plain_meaning: For us perfection is the summit of a graded ascent, not a state of being without fault. It is the declared subject of the Institutes, "the attainment of the perfect life." It is reached "not ... simply by self-denial ... unless there is that charity," climbed "from this fear to hope, from hope to the love of God." And at the summit we confess it is a thing "we cannot even make the effort to obtain ... without the mercy and inspiration of God."
glosses.quick_meaning: The summit of a graded ascent - fear, then hope, then love - with charity as its substance. Not flawlessness, and never reached without grace.
glosses.translational_sense: 'Perfection - do you mean sinlessness, an impossible standard?' - no: a graded ascent with charity as its substance and love at its top, measured by a goal rather than by faultlessness, whose stages are fear, hope and love, and whose summit is the confession that neither the effort nor the understanding of the effort is one's own; at Tours, simply a word of praise.
false_friend: perfectionism - flawlessness, sinlessness, an impossible standard producing anxiety
the perfect as an elite class
a Pelagian claim to be without sin

glosses.plain_meaning: In Cassian's Marseilles, discretion is the virtue by which every other is kept from destroying itself. It is "the mother of all virtues, as well as their guardian and regulator," the "eye and light of the body," the "royal road" between excess and slackness. It is gained "only ... by true humility." That means testing every thought, like a good money-changer testing coin, against the judgment of the elders.
glosses.quick_meaning: The virtue that keeps every other virtue from ruining itself. The royal road between excess and slackness, gained only by showing one's thoughts to the elders.
glosses.translational_sense: 'Discretion - you mean tact, or knowing when to keep quiet?' - no: the regulator of all the virtues, awarded that title by a council of Egyptian fathers, whose whole substance is the elders' judgment received through humility and disclosure, a money-changer's test of every thought on a royal road where "extremes meet" - a gift of grace, not a temperament.
false_friend: tact, prudence, or confidentiality
discernment as a private spiritual intuition or a decision-making technique
moderation as common sense

glosses.plain_meaning: For us the profession is the monastic undertaking as a binding public commitment, with its own "goal and end." A soldier makes it when he "professed himself a monk." A false monk assumes it "under the profession of a monk." A man "turned out a deserter or lukewarm" has betrayed it.
glosses.quick_meaning: The monk's binding, public undertaking of a whole way of life. Sworn like a soldier's oath, and betrayed like a deserter.
glosses.translational_sense: 'Did monks take formal vows, like a religious order today?' - not a canonical rite: a public undertaking of a whole way of life, with its own goal and end and its own "responsibility," sworn at Tours like a soldier's oath and betrayed as a soldier deserts, and capable of being assumed falsely "before the face of men."

the later formal rite of solemn vows with canonical consequences

confidence.divergence_note: Single-voice for the technical term (Cassian) - the most consequential single-voice term in the lexicon - and framed by Cassian himself as Abbot Moses's teaching received from Egypt; Doc_04 rates the attribution of this content to Gaul as Inferential, resting only on Gallic monks having been formed by it. The bare lemma puritas occurs once in Hilary of Arles's own Latin in a non-technical phrase of praise for Honoratus. Tours has the thing without the word. Conferences XII "On Chastity" is excised from the vendored edition - a gap inside this term's own content, stated rather than filled.

Cross-voice: the word and the act are shared across both nodes and a fourth voice (Salvian, who also uses it of the baptismal renunciation every Christian made at the font); the threefold schema is Cassian's alone and framed as Paphnutius's Egyptian teaching. Tours has the thing counselled and done without the technical term. Pruned from Doc_03's Tier-1 estimate because it does not organize independently of the pattern in which the renunciant returns to the Church as a bishop.

Weighted to Cassian: the technical sense is his and received (Moses, Paphnutius, Chaeremon, Nesteros); Sulpitius uses the word only as ordinary praise, and there is no doctrine of perfection at Tours in what was read. Two coverage limits bear on this term and are not filled: Conf. XXIII ("sinlessness") is unread and Conf. XII "On Chastity" is excised. The Latin perfectio is not attested in the vendored translation.

Single-voice (Cassian), and its content is Egypt's by Cassian's own framing - the verdict of "the blessed Antony and the other fathers" in a desert council; Doc_04 attributes it to Gaul only because Gallic monks were formed by it. Pruned from Doc_03's Tier-1 estimate as the closest call in Doc_06: no Doc_05 lens is organized by it, and the south's regulation actually operates through disclosure to the senior and the elders' judgment. Cassian awards "mother / mistress of all virtues" both to discretion and to humility - the title is not discretion's alone. Tours has the thing (Martin's refusals) without the word. The Latin discretio is not attested in the vendored translation; it occurs several times in the Faustus file by grep only, sense unread.

Both nodes, two voices: Sulpitius of individuals and oaths, Cassian of the whole way of life. The "goal and end" of the profession is Abbot Moses's teaching and received. The Latin professio is attested in the volume only in the editor's textual footnote to De Incarnatione, an unread work, and not in this sense.

results.message: Why did your people believe this?

voice_event.speaker: gallic
voice_event.text:
We believed it because that is how Christ showed himself to us - in the beggar's half of a soldier's cloak, and in the strangers an elder fed. The Lord chose the unpitied beggar at a city gate to reveal himself in, and the soldier saw him that night wearing the half he had given away. Among the brethren at Marseilles the fathers of Egypt taught the same thing: an elder broke his fast for two strangers at his door, because, he said, receiving Christ in you I ought to refresh him. He did not ask them what they were. What he taught that mattered most among us was that what is done to the least of these is done to him - the words Sulpitius set beside the cloak. And when Martin faced a devil dressed in purple and gold who said, I am Christ, he answered that he would not believe unless the one who came showed the marks of his wounds. That is the Christ we knew: the crucified one, met in the poor, whose form is the form in which he suffered.

**Sulpitius Severus, Life of St. Martin III**: At one point, he owned nothing but his weapons and his plain soldier's cloak. In the middle of a winter that had been harder than usual - so much so that many were dying from the extreme cold - he happened to meet a poor man at the gate of the city of Amiens. The man had no clothes. He was begging everyone who passed to have pity on him, but they all walked by. Then Martin, filled with God, understood that this man, to whom no one else showed mercy, was left for him. But what should he do? He had nothing but the cloak he was wearing. He had already given everything else away for the same purpose. So he took the sword he was wearing at his side, cut the cloak in two, gave half to the poor man, and put the other half back on. Some of the bystanders began to laugh, because he looked odd with his cloak cut short. But many others, who thought more soundly, groaned deeply at themselves. They had done nothing of the kind, though they had more and could have clothed the man without leaving themselves naked. That night, when Martin had fallen asleep, he saw Christ. Christ was wearing the half of his cloak with which he had covered the poor man. Martin looked carefully at the Lord, and at the garment he had given. Then he heard Jesus say in a clear voice to the crowd of angels standing around him: Martin, still a catechumen, has covered me with this cloak.

confidence.divergence_note: Documented as an author and a corpus - the Life (c. 397), the three undisputed Letters, the Dialogues (c. 404-406), the Sacred History - and independently by Gennadius ch. XIX (ancient text), who also records that "in his old age, he was led astray by the Pelagians" and kept penitent silence until death: a contested biographical datum in Gennadius's own voice, carried as such and not a contest about anything Sulpitius wrote. His dates rest only on the two modern editors' disagreeing endnotes (Roberts; Richardson), not on any ancient text, and are not asserted here. "Of an illustrious family," by the vendored volume's own introduction; his own text says he had his information "partly from himself ... and partly from those who had lived with him" (Vita ch. XXV) and disclaims presence at every event he narrates that these records carry. The Doubtful Letters to Claudia (row 5) are pseudepigraphal and are not drawn on. Every locus below read directly at Doc_09.

Weighted to Sulpitius (Tours) - angels are Martin's visitors and messengers; at Marseilles the angel chiefly spoken of is the devil's counterfeit, plus the two angels of the Shepherd. The historicity of the northern visitations is carried by virtus / power's Reported-Experience Status, not here.

results.message: Tell me about someone who lived this out.

voice_event.speaker: gallic
voice_event.text:
Paphnutius did. A young monk in Egypt, raised in the desert from boyhood, he was accused before the whole assembly of elders of stealing another brother's book. The accuser had hidden his own book in Paphnutius's cell out of jealousy. The book was found there. Paphnutius said nothing in his own defense. He asked the abbot for a plan of repentance and did public penance for a theft he had not committed. He bore it silently until God vindicated him: the accuser was seized by a demon and could only confess his lie and be healed by the man he had wronged. That is how the fathers of Egypt, as Cassian carried their stories to us, showed what a heart cleared to charity looks like - a man who said nothing for himself, asked how to repent for what he had not done, and waited for God rather than his own defense. The story came to Marseilles in a book. At Tours we had it differently: a presbyter Martin raised stormed into the courtyard, called his master's visions ridiculous fancies, and was borne with afterward because, Martin said, if Christ bore with Judas he could bear with this man.

**Cassian, Institutes IV.30**: This man wanted to spoil his beauty with some flaw or stain. The reason was that he was jealous of the boy's growing grace and goodness, and of the praise everyone was giving him. So he hid his own book, a book of the Gospels, in Paphnutius's cell. Then he accused him before all the brothers and elders of having stolen it. The boy's cell was searched. The book was found hidden there. Paphnutius knew his conscience was completely clear. Yet he said nothing to clear himself or to accuse the man who was falsely charging him. He asked the abbot for a plan of repentance, and did penance for the theft he had not committed.

glosses.plain_meaning: The man whose judgment stands in for the junior's own - the senior to whom every thought is laid bare, and by whose "examination" a thing is "good or bad." "Abbot" is the title of every Egyptian father Cassian reports. At Tours the same place is held by one master, Martin, who himself consults "his elders, whether among the presbyters or clerics."
glosses.quick_meaning: The senior whose judgment replaces the junior's own, to whom every thought is shown. "Abbot" is an Egyptian father's title; at Tours it is one master with no title at all.
glosses.translational_sense: 'So the abbot was the boss - like a Benedictine abbot with a crozier?' - no: for Cassian "Abbot" is the honorific of an Egyptian father, never applied in what survives to a Gallic superior; what matters is the senior's examination of every thought, which replaces one's own judgment, and at Tours a master obeyed without a rule, who himself defers to "his elders" on what antiquity allows.
false_friend: abbot as the canonical head of a Benedictine abbey, elected for life, with jurisdiction and a crozier
elder as a church officer or simply an old man
the senior's judgment of thoughts as spiritual direction or counselling one may take or leave

glosses.plain_meaning: The public discipline of our house. For a fault, a monk lies on the ground until the Abbot bids him rise, or is barred from prayer with the brethren. No priest is needed to restore him.
glosses.quick_meaning: The house's public discipline. For a small fault, on the ground until the Abbot bids you rise; for more, barred from prayer with the brethren; for the worst, stripes or expulsion. At Tours, the master's prayer brings the sinner back.
glosses.translational_sense: A modern hearer thinks of private confession, a formula of absolution, and assigned penances. Ours is public, bodily, and ended by the elder's word: on the ground until the Abbot bids rise, excluded from the brethren's prayer, beaten or expelled for the worst - and, at Tours, a repentance brought about by the master's prayer.

"penance" as self-punishment
"satisfaction" as a scholastic category

confidence.divergence_note: Cross-voice in the title: the function is shared across both nodes, but the title "Abbot" is Cassian's Egyptian usage, never applied in what survives to a Gallic superior (who merely "presides"); the one Gallic house whose head is called abbot, Lerins, is so called only by Gennadius c. 495. The deans, steward and guest-Elder are prescriptions whose Gallic uptake Cassian himself doubts (Inst. IV.2), and Lerins's internal grades are not attested. The Latin abbas is not supplied against the text.

Weighted to Cassian - the graded institutional penance (public penance on the ground until the Abbot bids rise; suspension from prayer; stripes or expulsion) is Egypt's prescription by Cassian's own framing, and whether any Gallic house kept the grades is not documented. Tours has a repentance of persons (Brictio; the soldiers' conscience) and no written grade. Coverage limit: Conf. XX "On true satisfaction in repentance," whose title Gennadius attests, is unread. Latin not supplied against the text; baucalis is Cassian's own transliterated word.

voice_event.speaker: gallic
voice_event.text:
That power in the Church, among us, was a thing both shown and refused at once, and we never settled which was right. At Tours the saint had more power as a monk than as a bishop, and after one forced communion to save men from the sword he felt his power lessen and never attended a synod again. The bishops who made him one had bowed to the emperor's court; in Martin alone apostolic authority kept its place. Yet those same bishops were the ones who guarded the faith. On the island Vincent held that an ancient council's decree should be preferred over the rashness of a few, and named the twofold authority of the Apostolic See. And among the brethren at Marseilles the fathers taught that wanting holy orders was vainglory's own suggestion. So bishops guard the truth and the monk flees the office - and then the Church comes for him anyway, and he keeps a monk's life inside a see. We honoured the office and distrusted wanting it. We produced bishops and fled synods. That tension never resolved, and it is the shape our whole life kept.

**Sulpitius Severus, Vita XX**: Among all those bishops, Martin alone kept himself free from the alliances and intrigues they were all caught up in. To the very end, he kept up his own authority. And even if he could not stop what was being done, he at least took no part in doing it. Apostolic authority, then, would truly have been seen in Martin alone among them all, if the character and power of an Apostle had not been wanting in him. Meanwhile the bishops had given way weakly with a degenerate submissiveness. They were daily in communion with Ithacius, who had become unbearably boastful and swollen with pride because of his alliance with the imperial court. In Martin alone, apostolic authority kept its place.

glosses.plain_meaning: The office our monks keep being taken into. A monk "carried off," "escorted under guard," "bound to the long-avoided office," who then keeps "the objects and virtues of a monk" in a see. And at the same time our own formation teaching names the desire for that office as vainglory's suggestion and the devil's pretext.
glosses.quick_meaning: The office our monks are seized into and must never seek. Fled, then overtaken; kept with a monk's humility; costing the saint some of his power.
glosses.translational_sense: 'Wasn't becoming a bishop either a promotion or a sell-out for a monk?' - neither, for us: the office was something one was seized into by a crowd, a trick, or a "fillet," it cost the saint his power, our own formation manual named wanting it as vainglory, and inside it a monk kept "the objects and virtues of a monk" - and a bishop's singular teaching still counted for nothing against the consent of the ancients.
false_friend: a bishop as an administrator or prelate
monk and bishop as opposed careers, so that a monk-bishop is either a promotion or a sell-out
Pope as the bishop of Rome only
episcopal election as a formal procedure

glosses.plain_meaning: Chiefly the bond of fellowship. To withhold it is the Church's sharpest sanction; to extend it wrongly defiles. Martin's one forced communion cost him power. A monk at fault loses his place at prayer.
glosses.quick_meaning: The bond of fellowship, with real weight. Withheld from bishops who urged the sword; forced once on Martin and paid for in lost power; lost by a monk at fault until he does penance. The sacrament sits inside it.
glosses.translational_sense: A modern hearer thinks first of the eucharistic rite, or of a denominational "communion," or of excommunication as a legal penalty. For us communion is fellowship with spiritual weight - refused to bishops who urged the sword, forced once and paid for in diminished power, lost by a fault and restored by penance on the ground.

glosses.plain_meaning: Two things at once. At Lerins, the ancients' decree that guards the faith, legitimate because it innovates nothing. At Tours, the assembly of bishops that handed heretics to the sword, and that Martin never entered again.
glosses.quick_meaning: For Vincent, the ancients' decree preferred to the rashness of a few, valid because it adds nothing. For Martin, the assembly that handed heretics to the sword, and which he never attended again. Two hearings we never reconciled.
glosses.translational_sense: A modern hearer wants a council to be a constitutional organ with defined authority, or wants Martin's refusal to be a stand against institutions. Neither fits. For Vincent a council is legitimate only because it hands on what it received; for Martin the synod is where bishops urged the sword, and he would not sit there again.
false_friend: "ecumenical council" as a settled constitutional organ with defined authority
synods as church bureaucracy
Martin's refusal as anti-institutionalism

glosses.plain_meaning: At Tours, the highest thing said of Martin - having the apostles' power over death, demons, and emperors. At Marseilles, the perfection of love, and the first Church's common life.
glosses.quick_meaning: At Tours, the highest word for Martin - the apostles' own power, shown by raising the dead and facing an emperor. At Marseilles, the perfection of love, and the common life of the first Church.
glosses.translational_sense: A modern hearer may reach for "apostolic succession" - a doctrine of orders - or for an institutional adjective. Neither is ours. For us "apostolic" means the apostles' own power possessed by a living saint, or the perfection of love the ascent reaches, or the antiquity of the common life.
false_friend: "apostolic succession" as a doctrine of validly ordained bishops
"apostolic" as an institutional or denominational adjective
Martin's "apostolic authority" as jurisdiction

glosses.plain_meaning: "Pope" is a title of honour we give to bishops we revere - Cassian's Pope Castor of Apta Julia. "The Apostolic See" is Vincent's Rome, foremost in refusing novelty. Not the same relation.
glosses.quick_meaning: "Pope" is how we honour any revered bishop - Cassian writes to Pope Castor of Provence. "The Apostolic See" is Vincent's Rome, weighty because it refused novelty. Two words, two relations.
glosses.translational_sense: A modern hearer hears "Pope" and thinks of one office in one city. Among us the title was a Western bishop's honour, and Rome's claim, when Vincent makes it, is that its bishops were foremost in guarding what was handed down - not a constitutional supremacy read back from later centuries.
false_friend: "Pope" as the bishop of Rome exclusively, with the later constitutional office read back
Vincent as a proof-text for papal supremacy
Cassian's "Pope Castor" as an error

sentences.sentence: That power in the Church, among us, was a thing both shown and refused at once, and we never settled which was right.

sentences.sentence: At Tours the saint had more power as a monk than as a bishop, and after one forced communion to save men from the sword he felt his power lessen and never attended a synod again.
The bishops who made him one had bowed to the emperor's court; in Martin alone apostolic authority kept its place.
Yet those same bishops were the ones who guarded the faith.
On the island Vincent held that an ancient council's decree should be preferred over the rashness of a few, and named the twofold authority of the Apostolic See.
And among the brethren at Marseilles the fathers taught that wanting holy orders was vainglory's own suggestion.
So bishops guard the truth and the monk flees the office - and then the Church comes for him anyway, and he keeps a monk's life inside a see.
sentences.why: tagged claim, shares ground with its own records

sentences.sentence: We honoured the office and distrusted wanting it.
We produced bishops and fled synods.
That tension never resolved, and it is the shape our whole life kept.
**Sulpitius Severus, Vita XX**: Among all those bishops, Martin alone kept himself free from the alliances and intrigues they were all caught up in.

confidence.divergence_note: Cross-voice tension by design, marked [PV]: the Egyptian sources Cassian carries treat the office as a temptation (vainglory's wish for holy orders; the devil's pretext), while the Gallic reception in which Cassian, Sulpitius and Hilary of Arles all write treats monk-to-bishop as the destination. Both valences are ours and must stay audible. Hilary's Latin for Honoratus's capture is Doc_04's rendering of rough OCR (wording Inferential/Thin; presence checked by grep). Mathisen's account of the Lerins episcopal network is thesis-level only, and Lerins's own internal life remains the least-documented institution; this record does not fill that gap. The Sulpitius-Pelagianism charge (Gennadius ch. XIX) is a contested biographical datum, not a contest about this term.

No Author Gravity - all three founding voices, both nodes: ecclesial fellowship with consequences in the saint's body at Tours; suspension from prayer at Marseilles; "the unity of communion and of the faith" at Lerins. The one thing this term cannot state from a Native text as read is the sacrament's frequency in Gaul: Gibson's footnote claiming daily communion in Gaul cites a chapter of the book his own edition omits entirely (Inst. VI.viii) - an editor's claim resting on an unread Latin text, carried as editorial and Inferential/Thin, not as our own statement. Latin communionis is attested only in Heurtley's editorial appendix.

Cross-voice tension, directly opposed [PV]: the same institution is the guarantor of truth in Vincent's Lerins (an ancient General Council's decrees preferred to "the rashness and ignorance of a few"; Ephesus, which "innovated nothing") and the thing the saint flees in Sulpitius's Tours (the assembly of bishops that handed the Priscillianists to the sword; "never again did he attend a synod"). The divergence is the finding, not a defect, and the two hearings are never reconciled. Cassian has no council in what was read. No Latin lemma sought.

Widely Accepted at the narrative level: one named, socially located author, in two of his own works - not two converging accounts of one event. Sacred History II.50 narrates an earlier phase (Martin's plea at Treves before Priscillian's execution); Dialogues III.11-13 narrates a later visit after the execution, with the coerced communion, Felix's ordination, and the angel; the two share an author, a setting, and a principle. Contested for the angel's speech and for the diminution of power, which are Martin's own reported experience ("he at once confessed to us with tears") as Sulpitius transmits it through Gallus. Sulpitius's hostile characterization of Ithacius ("no worth or holiness about him," SH II.50) is his own perspective. Registry row 6 (Sacred History) is rated B on a "narrative text not read" session note; II.50 was read directly at Doc_04 and re-read at Doc_09 - a fresh verification the source record's own state does not yet reflect. The text gives no year; Gallus says only that Martin "lived sixteen years after this." Roberts's note on the corrupt text at "Andethanna" is editorial. confidence.divergence_note: Documented as an author and a date: the Commonitory dates itself three years after the Council of Ephesus, to 434 (Doc_01 §2.3), and Gennadius ch. LXV (ancient text) records the work, the pseudonym, and the theft of "the greater part of the second book." Widely Accepted for the attribution to Vincentius. Contested whether he held or only sympathized with the Massilian position (Doc_02 §1); whether "Peregrinus" conceals anything is not settled by any Native text. His death is placed "before 450, and probably shortly after 434" on Gennadius's regnal formula (Doc_01 §2.4); his entry to Lerins is undated - "c. 425" is Inferential-Thin, a floating convention (Doc_01 §2.3) - and the claim that he was brother to Lupus of Troyes is Inferential-Thin and uncorroborated by Gennadius. Of the island he says only that he dwells "in the seclusion of a Monastery." Salvian (row 43) is not licensed for grace-related material and is not drawn on for him.

Cross-voice in referent: Vincent's "Apostolic See" is Rome (Lerins); Cassian's "Pope" is a Gallic bishop - Castor of Apta Julia, Leontius (Marseilles). The two do not conflict, because the word is a title in one and a see in the other. The Marseilles resistance to Celestine's letter ("clung to their views in spite of the authority of the Pope") is known only at editorial strength, through Gibson's prolegomena. Latin papa is supplied by Gibson's editorial footnote, which itself states the title "was not limited to the Bishop of Rome till a later date." Sulpitius calls Liberius simply "bishop of the city of Rome," in a chapter located by grep and not read in full.
